title: Hydraulic Ironworker Machines, 44 to 276 Ton | NovoTech
meta_description: Hydraulic ironworkers, 44–276 US tons: punch, shear bar, angle and flat, notch. HKM single- and double-piston, plus the NovoTech value-line Q35Y.
intro: A hydraulic ironworker (also sold as a steelworker or universal punch and shear) puts the five jobs of the structural shop on one machine: punching, round and square bar shear, angle shear at 90° and 45°, flat-bar and sheet shear and rectangular notching, each with its own station and LED light. The HKM range runs from the 44 US ton HKM 40 to the 193 US ton HKM 175 in two designs: single-piston machines in which one cylinder serves every station — compact and economical — and double-piston machines with two cylinders and two foot pedals so two operators punch and shear at the same time. Punches to Ø1-1/2″ are standard on every model; large-hole, section punching, beam and tee blades, V-notching, press-brake and keyway tools are optional. Below the NovoTech premium-line machines is NovoTech's own value line, the Q35Y single-cylinder ironworkers from 55 to 276 US tons, built in China to our specification and sold under our name with the tooling included. All sold with a CSA-approved panel and installed, tooled and supported from Mississauga, ON, Canada.

faq.a: A single-piston machine (HKM 40 – 65 V) uses one hydraulic cylinder for all stations, so one operator works one station at a time — the right choice for a fabrication shop that punches a few holes and cuts a few angles per job. A double-piston machine (HKM 55 – 175) has two cylinders and two foot pedals, so one operator can punch while another shears or notches: twice the output from one machine, plus an electrical back gauge as standard.

faq.q: What size ironworker do I need?
faq.a: Size it by the thickest material you punch and the largest angle you shear. The punching capacity is quoted as a hole diameter × thickness at the machine's tonnage — a 66 US ton HKM 60 punches Ø1-1/8″ through 9/16″ plate and shears L 4-3/4 × 4-3/4 × 1/2″ angle; the HKM 115 punches Ø1-3/8″ × 1″ and shears L 5-7/8 × 5-7/8 × 5/8″. Tell us your plate thickness, largest angle and flat bar and we will point to the model on the capacity table.

faq.q: What tooling comes with the machine?
faq.a: A Ø7/8″ punch and die (Ø1″ on the HKM 115), the round and square bar blade set, the angle blade set, the flat-bar shear blades and — except on the HKM 40 — the rectangular notching blade set. Punches and dies to Ø1-1/2″ in any diameter, oblong or square are stocked in Mississauga, ON, Canada; large-hole punching sets go to Ø4-7/8″ with the optional tool.

faq.q: Can an ironworker cut channel, I-beam and tee?
faq.a: Yes, with the optional section blades on the shear station — UPN and IPN sections up to 11-3/4 × 4-7/8″ and tee to 5-7/8 × 9/16″ on the HKM 175 — and the section punching tools punch the flanges and webs of IPN, UPN, flat bar and angle.

faq.q: Ironworker or band saw for cutting angle?
faq.a: An ironworker shears a 4″ angle in one stroke and a few seconds, with no blade to wear and no chips; the cut is square with a slight deformation at the edge. A band saw takes a minute per cut but leaves a clean, mitre-capable cut on any section. Shops that cut hundreds of angles and flats a day keep both: the ironworker for brackets, clips and base plates, the saw for mitres and beams.

faq.q: What voltage do these machines run on?
faq.a: Three-phase machines are supplied for 600 V as standard with a CSA-approved panel; 208 V, 240 V and 480 V 3-phase are available on request, and 240 V single-phase on models whose main motor is 2.2 kW (3 HP) or less — a machine with a motor above 2.2 kW must run on three-phase power and cannot be converted to 240 V single-phase. Manual machines have no electrics.
